strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear empirical demonstration of error recovery gap between model scales (Figure 1)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with consistent improvements and strong baselines (GRPO, DAPO, Dr.GRPO)
Thorough ablation studies effectively isolating the contribution of fission mechanism (+1.25%) from error simulator quality (+3.62%)
High-quality data construction with hierarchical filtering, consensus verification, and detailed case studies supporting reproducibility
Sound technical approach: three-stage pipeline is well-motivated and the Error Simulator design avoids target leakage through non-revealing error descriptions
Clear presentation of algorithm with pseudocode and prompting templates; qualitative analysis shows interpretable progression from collapse to active diagnosis
Sensitivity analysis on correction trigger frequency demonstrates practical understanding of computational trade-offs
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: single benchmark (BFCL v4 Multi-Turn) with no evaluation on other tool-use benchmarks or domains despite generalization claims; unclear if results transfer to other error distributions or real-world APIs

Computational overhead inadequately addressed: no timing comparisons, FLOPs analysis, or wall-clock measurements; claims that overhead is 'partially mitigated' through trigger frequency N lack supporting cost-benefit quantification

Error Simulator quality and generalization insufficiently analyzed: no evaluation of simulator accuracy, analysis of generalization to novel error types during training, or assessment of failure modes; simulator is Qwen3-32B (large model dependency)

On-policy approximation claims are loose: errors are collected in Stage 1 and resampled in Stage 3 creating lag; LIFO helps but formal distribution shift analysis (KL divergence, importance weighting) is absent
Reward design appears ad-hoc: time-dependent weight schedules (wfmt: 2→1, wcorr: 2→3, Rlen piecewise Gaussian) lack justification or ablation studies; no sensitivity analysis to weight choices

Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests reported; with stochastic RL and ~630 training instances, point estimates alone are insufficient (e.g., 46.75% vs 44.88% vs Dr.GRPO unclear if meaningful)
Generalization concerns: all experiments on Qwen3 family only; unclear applicability to other model families, RL algorithms beyond GRPO, or domains beyond tool-use

Missing relevant comparisons: no baselines for simpler error-handling strategies (rejection sampling, prompt-based retry, rule-based handlers) or empirical comparison with other recent error-driven synthesis methods

strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling empirical evidence (Figure 1b); clear gap between small (Qwen3-8B ~20%) and large (Claude Sonnet ~50%) model error recovery rates
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three benchmarks (BFCL v4, TAU-Bench, TAU2-Bench), multiple model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B), and strong baselines (GRPO, DAPO, Dr.GRPO, AWPO)

Thorough ablations isolating Error Simulator contribution (Table 2), compute-matched comparison (Table 4) validating efficiency gains, and cross-domain evaluation with human validation (96% non-leakage, Cohen's κ=0.71)
Consistent improvements across settings: 5.7% error recovery gain for Qwen3-8B, 4.0% overall accuracy (42.75%→46.75%), with gains up to +17.4% on TAU benchmarks
Thoughtful framework design with hybrid feedback synthesis, LIFO buffering, and principled data curation (630 high-quality instances from hierarchical filtering pipeline)
Strong reproducibility: detailed Algorithm 1, prompt templates, hyperparameter documentation, and promised code release
Effective qualitative analysis (Figure 7) illustrating progression from model collapse → hallucination → active diagnosis, providing interpretable insights beyond metrics
weaknesses: Critical concern about Error Simulator requiring ground-truth tool calls (τgt) at inference time; unclear how this constraint is satisfied in deployment, and claim of 'preventing target leakage' contradicts conditioning on τgt

Limited algorithmic novelty: core mechanism is straightforward resampling from augmented contexts with supervised feedback generation—incremental integration into GRPO rather than fundamental innovation

Error Simulator trained on only ~2K synthetic examples with single teacher (Claude Sonnet 4); no comparison with alternative error feedback methods; potential for teacher bias; robustness to out-of-distribution errors unclear

Critical design choices lack justification: LIFO buffering vs. alternatives (FIFO, random), reward component ablations (Eq. 2), trigger interval N setting, and correctness threshold δcorr=1 all set empirically without systematic analysis
No statistical significance testing: results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed validation; improvements of 4-5% in some categories may not be robust to initialization variance

Incomplete baseline comparisons: ToolACE and LoopTool cited as related but not directly compared; only RL baselines included; external agent results show unusual patterns (0.9% on TAU Retail) suggesting potential evaluation issues

Limited domain coverage in evaluation: three benchmarks share similar tool-calling structure; all training data synthetically generated; real API error distributions and deployment scenarios not tested
Uneven performance across error categories (Miss Param: 38% for 8B vs. Base: 57.5%), no failure mode analysis, and unclear when/why method underperforms suggest incomplete understanding
Scalability to larger models (13B+) unclear; unknown whether error recovery naturally improves with scale, making the method's general applicability uncertain

Insufficient ablations on reward design (time-dependent weighting, α=0.5), LIFO strategy justification, and sensitivity analysis of critical hyperparameters (N, δcorr) raise concerns about design choices
